concepts.title: focal length

- Determines lens focusing properties.

concepts.title: Lensmaker's formula generalization for different radii of curvature
concepts.one_liner: The generalized Lensmaker's formula for a lens with different radii of curvature is $$\frac{1}{f} = (n-1) \left( \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2} \right)$$.
concepts.content:
One can generalize the equation for the case of a lens with different radii of curvature, $R_1$ and $R_2$, on the front and back faces of the lens. Defining the left and right surface angles $\theta_{s_1}$ and $\theta_{s_2}$ respectively, the middle row equation of table @tbl-lensmaker becomes $\theta_{s_1} + \theta_{s_2} = \theta_2 + \theta_3$. Then, the equation substitutions of Table @tbl-lensmaker, combined with $\theta_{S_i} = c / R_i$ for $i = 1$ and $2$, lead to

$$\frac{1}{f} = (n-1) \left( \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2} \right)$$

concepts.title: Snell's Law
concepts.one_liner: Snell's Law relates the angles of incident and refracted light rays at a material boundary using indices of refraction.
concepts.content:
At a material boundary, for the geometry illustrated in @fig-snell, we have
$$n_1 \sin(\theta_1) = n_2 \sin(\theta_2)$$
where $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$ are the angles with respect to the surface normal of the incident and outgoing light rays, and $n_1$ and $n_2$ are the indices of refraction of the materials in region 1 and region 2. Snell's law can be derived by matching the wavelength of light projected along the material interface boundary across each side of the boundary.

concepts.title: Demonstration of focusing property for a thin lens
concepts.one_liner: All the light rays that strike the lens are focused to the same green spot, while rays passing outside reveal their straight line trajectories.
concepts.content:
@fig-greenLaser shows a demonstration of the focusing property for a thin lens. The hand, labeled (a), flicks a laser pointer back and forth, sending light rays in many directions from a central point during the image exposure, as would a diffuse surface reflection. All the light rays that strike the lens, labeled (b), are focused to the same green spot, labeled (c), while the light rays passing outside the lens at (b) reveal their straight line trajectories on the wall at (c).

![Demonstration showing that a lens focuses a fan of rays, such as those reflecting from a diffuse surface, to a point. (a) Here the right hand wiggles a laser pointer back and forth during the photographic exposure, generating a fan of light rays, approximating (in one dimension) rays reflecting from one point on a diffuse surface. (b) The fan of rays sweeps across a lens, which focuses each ray passing through the lens to the same spot at the wall, (c), regardless of where each ray had entered the lens. (c) The rays that pass outside the lens form the two line segments on either side.](figures/imaging/greenLaserBrightenedCrop2.jpg){#fig-greenLaser width="90%"}
concepts.motivation_md: This demonstration visually confirms the fundamental focusing property of lenses, showing how rays from a point source converge to a single point after passing through a lens, which is essential for image formation.
concepts.recap_md:
- A thin lens focuses all rays from a point source to a single point.
- Rays passing outside the lens continue in straight lines.
- The demonstration uses a laser pointer flicked to simulate diffuse reflection.

concepts.title: convex lens
concepts.one_liner: Light passing through the center of a thin lens, where the front and back surfaces are parallel, proceeds without bending.
concepts.content:
Armed with the lensmaker's formula and the observation of @fig-thinLens, we can analyze how rays travel through lenses in the approximation of geometrical optics. Light passing through the center of a thin lens, where the front and back surfaces are parallel, proceeds without bending. concepts.title: Properties of light travel through lenses
concepts.one_liner: Light from one conjugate point traveling through the lens focuses to the other conjugate point, and parallel rays focus to the focal point at distance $f$.
concepts.content:
Two points on opposite sides of the lens at distances $a$ and $b$ from the lens that satisfy @eq-lensmaker are known as conjugate points. Light from one conjugate point, traveling through the lens, focuses to the other conjugate point, and vice versa (see @fig-lenspropt). The rules for tracing light travel through a lens include the following:

1.  Every ray passing through one conjugate point and passing through the lens then passes through the conjugate point. This is the fundamental focusing property of a lens.

2.  Parallel rays entering the lens all focus to a point at distance $f$ behind the lens, per @eq-lensmaker. In this case, one of the focal points is at infinity.

3.  Any ray passing through the center of the thin lens proceeds in a straight line, as if through a pinhole at the center of the lens (see @fig-thinLens). Thus, lenses, like pinholes, render the world in *perspective projection*.

4.  Because focused rays render positions onto a plane as does a line passing through the center of the lens, then the **magnification** of a lens is simply $a/b$, where $a$ is the distance of an infocus object to the lens, and $b$ is the distance from the lens to a sensor plane.
concepts.motivation_md: These properties summarize how lenses focus light and form images, which is fundamental to understanding optical systems and image magnification.
concepts.recap_md:
- Conjugate points satisfy the lensmaker's formula and focus light reciprocally.
- Parallel rays focus at the focal point distance $f$ behind the lens.
- Rays through the lens center proceed straight, producing perspective projection.
- Magnification is the ratio $a/b$ of object and sensor distances.

concepts.title: depth of field formula
concepts.one_liner: Defining the depth of field, $D$, to be $D = D_1 + D_2$, and combining terms, we have $$D = \frac{2 N C U^2 f^2}{f^4 - N^2 C^2 U^2}$$.
concepts.content:
By similar triangles, we have $$\frac{D_1 f}{C U} = \frac{U - D_1}{\frac{f}{N}}$$ and also $$\frac{D_2 f}{C U} = \frac{D_2+U}{\frac{f}{N}}.$$ Defining the depth of field, $D$, to be $D = D_1 + D_2$, and combining terms, we obtain
$$D = \frac{2 N C U^2 f^2}{f^4 - N^2 C^2 U^2}.$$ When the circle of confusion, $C$, is much smaller than the lens aperture, $f/N$, then the term $N^2 C^2 D^2$ can be ignored relative to $f^4$, giving the approximation
$$D \approx \frac{2 N C U^2}{f^2}.$$ Note that for smaller camera apertures, this approximation holds well.
concepts.motivation_md: The depth of field formula quantifies the range over which objects appear acceptably sharp in an image, helping photographers understand how aperture, focal length, and focus distance affect image sharpness.

- Exact formula: $D = \frac{2 N C U^2 f^2}{f^4 - N^2 C^2 U^2}$.
- Approximate formula when $C$ is small: $D \approx \frac{2 N C U^2}{f^2}$.

concepts.title: concave lenses
concepts.one_liner: A concave lens has the lens surface curve bowing inward toward the center, causing parallel rays entering it to be bent away from the lens center and brought to a virtual focus.
concepts.content:
The lens designed previously was convex. Concave lenses, by contrast, have the lens surface curve bowing inward toward the center of the lens. For example, consider the concave lens with the surface orientation, $\theta_{Sx} = -\theta_S$. By reflection symmetry of the lens surface angles, parallel rays entering a concave lens are bent away from the lens center by the same amount they would be bent toward the center axis for a convex lens of the same radii of curvature. This causes a concave lens to bring parallel rays to a virtual focus, a point from which the diverging rays leaving the lens appear to emanate. This is illustrated in the figures showing on-axis and off-axis parallel rays.

(see figure: A ray diagram showing parallel light rays entering a concave lens from the left at a downward angle. The rays diverge upon exiting the lens, and dashed lines trace their paths backward to a single...)

The mathematics of ray bending is similar to convex lenses, except the focal length of concave lenses is negative. The focus point for parallel rays entering a concave lens from the left is on the left side of the lens. It is a virtual focal point, and from the right side of the lens, the emanating rays appear to originate from the point at distance $-f$ to the left of the lens.

concepts.title: Lenses in a Telescope
concepts.one_liner: The magnification of a Galilean telescope is the ratio $M = \frac{f_1}{f_2}$ of the focal lengths of the convex and concave lenses.
concepts.content:
The properties of convex and concave lenses can be used to make a telescope, as Galileo did in the early 1600s. We position a convex lens (lens 1) with a long focal length $f_1$ and a concave lens (lens 2) with a shorter focal length $f_2$ such that each is placed $f_1$ and $f_2$ away from a common point, respectively. Under these conditions, parallel rays from a distant object entering lens 1 become a compressed set of parallel rays leaving lens 2.

Referring to the angular deviations, an input ray angle deviation $\delta_i$ becomes an output angular deviation $\delta_o$ after passing through the telescope. Using the small angle approximation and properties of imaging with lenses, we have $\delta_i f_1 = d$ and $\delta_o f_2 = d$, where $d$ is the focal point offset.

Substituting for $d$ gives the telescope magnification,
$$M = \frac{\delta_o}{\delta_i} = \frac{f_1}{f_2},$$
which defines the amplification of the parallel ray bending angles.

(see figure: A ray diagram of a Galilean telescope consisting of two lenses. Parallel rays from the left pass through a convex lens (lens 1) and converge toward its focal point at distance $f_1$. Before reaching...)

(see figure: A ray diagram of a Galilean telescope featuring a convex lens (lens 1) and a concave lens (lens 2) aligned on a horizontal optical axis. Parallel rays enter lens 1 from the left at a small angle...)

Fig (a) Galilean telescope. The convex lens 1 and the concave lens 2 share the same focal point, marked with a dot, resulting in parallel rays in giving parallel rays out. (b) A small change in the input ray angle gives a larger change in the output ray angle. The magnification of the telescope is the ratio, $M$, of the angular deviation of an output ray, $\delta_o$, to the angular deviation of an input ray, $\delta_i$. Writing the focal point offset, $d$, in terms of the rays passing through the centers of lenses 1 and 2 gives the relation, $M = f_1/f_2$, where $f_1$ and $f_2$ are the respective ray focal lengths.

- Parallel rays entering lens 1 become compressed parallel rays leaving lens 2.
- The telescope magnification is $M = \frac{f_1}{f_2}$, the ratio of focal lengths.

concepts.title: Homemade Galilean telescope
concepts.one_liner: A homemade Galilean telescope uses a cardboard tube with two lenses, achieving magnification comparable to Galileo's original telescope.
concepts.content:
A homemade telescope inspired by Galileo's design uses a 2-inch cardboard mailing tube with a second smaller tube inserted inside to allow adjustment of the interlens distance for focusing. The convex lens at the front has a focal length of 50 cm, and the convex lens eyepiece has a focal length of 18 mm, giving a magnification of 27, comparable to Galileo's 30x magnification.

(see figure: A photograph of a homemade Galilean telescope constructed from two nested cardboard tubes. A convex glass lens is visible at the open end of the inner tube, secured in place with black tape.)

(see figure: A photograph of components for a homemade Galilean telescope on a wooden surface. It includes a long white cardboard tube with rubber bands and two separate white circular lens mounts, one containing...)

The two lenses are mounted in the cardboard tube, with focusing allowed by adjusting the inserted smaller tube holding the eyepiece lens. Rubber bands mount the telescope to a tripod, and the tube interior is lined with black paper to reduce stray light.

concepts.one_liner: Galileo's telescope revealed that the moon had mountains and craters, disproving the idea of a perfect sphere.
concepts.content:
Comparing images made from the homemade telescope with Galileo's drawings shows that he discovered the moon had mountains and craters, proving it was not a perfect sphere as previously thought. Although he could not resolve Saturn's rings, he noticed its unusual shape. These observations were possible with just two lenses within a tube.

concepts.one_liner: Lenses focus rays from a point on a surface to a single sensor position, creating images that are both sharp and bright, overcoming pinhole camera limitations.
concepts.content:
Pinhole cameras allow more light to enter the aperture only at the expense of image sharpness. Lenses overcome this tradeoff by focusing all rays passing through the lens from a point on a surface to a single position on the sensor plane, creating an image that is both sharp and bright.

Using small-angle and thin-lens approximations, we designed a lens surface to have that focusing property, showing the lens must have a parabolic or spherical shape.

Geometric considerations allow depth-of-field calculations and the design of a simple telescope.
